title: Two CTEs Together
story: You can chain CTEs with commas. Build small steps, then combine them.
goal: With CTEs spend (customer_id, spent for delivered orders) and avg_spend (one value avg), list the names of customers whose spend is above the average, alphabetically (column name).

tests.label: Hidden check on other data

hints: The second CTE can read the first one.
Compare s.spent with (SELECT avg FROM avg_spend).

WITH spend AS (SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.qty * p.price) AS spent FROM orders o JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY o.customer_id), avg_spend AS (SELECT AVG(spent) AS avg FROM spend) SELECT c.name FROM spend s JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id WHERE s.spent > (SELECT avg FROM avg_spend) ORDER BY c.name;
socratic: Which customers are missing because they have no delivered orders?
explain: In one sentence: what does this query do, and why does it need the two CTEs?
solution: WITH spend AS (SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.qty * p.price) AS spent FROM orders o JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY o.customer_id), avg_spend AS (SELECT AVG(spent) AS avg FROM spend) SELECT c.name FROM spend s JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id WHERE s.spent > (SELECT avg FROM avg_spend) ORDER BY c.name;
alt: WITH spend AS (SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.qty * p.price) AS spent FROM orders o JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY o.customer_id), avg_spend AS (SELECT AVG(spent) AS avg FROM spend) SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN spend s ON s.customer_id = c.id, avg_spend a WHERE s.spent > a.avg ORDER BY c.name;
